title: grep and regular expressions
goal: Find exactly the lines and values you need in logs and configs with grep options and regular expressions.
setup: # P1: backend log with a Java-style stack trace

printf '%s\n' '2026-10-20 09:00:01 INFO  OrderService started' '2026-10-20 09:02:15 INFO  GET /api/orders 200' '2026-10-20 09:02:16 WARN  retrying payment call' '2026-10-20 09:02:17 ERROR PaymentClient failed' 'java.net.SocketTimeoutException: Read timed out' '    at PaymentClient.call(PaymentClient.java:42)' '    at OrderService.pay(OrderService.java:88)' '2026-10-20 09:03:00 INFO  GET /api/orders 200' '2026-10-20 09:05:40 ERROR Database pool exhausted' '2026-10-20 09:05:41 INFO  pool size raised to 30' > logs/orders.log
# P2: configs that mention database hosts
# P3: nginx access log with response times
# P4: sshd-style config with comments and empty lines

printf '%s\n' '# Example SSH server config (practice copy)' '' 'Port 22' '#PermitRootLogin yes' 'PermitRootLogin no' '' '   # indented comment' 'PasswordAuthentication no' 'MaxAuthTries 3' > configs/sshd_config.copy

printf '%s\n' '2026-10-20 10:00:00 ERROR disk write failed' '2026-10-20 10:00:05 FATAL kernel panic on node-3' '2026-10-20 10:00:09 INFO request from 10.0.0.5' '2026-10-20 10:00:10 INFO request from 10.0.0.50' '2026-10-20 10:00:12 INFO request from 10a0b0c5' '2026-10-20 10:00:20 WARN Timeout calling api' '2026-10-20 10:00:21 WARN timeout calling db' > logs/node.log

printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/bash' '# 1) count lines with ERROR or FATAL' '# 2) show requests from the IP 10.0.0.5 only' '# 3) count timeout warnings (any case)' 'echo "errors: $(grep -c "ERROR|FATAL" logs/node.log)"' 'grep "10.0.0.5" logs/node.log' 'echo "timeouts: $(grep -c "timeout" logs/node.log)"' > alert.sh
printf '%s\n' '[ERROR] price is $5.00' 'ERROR price is 5x00' 'path a.b*c found' > special.txt

warmup.q: How does a function give back a string?
warmup.a: It prints it with `echo`; the caller catches it with `VAR=$(func)`. `return` is only for exit codes 0-255.

warmup.q: Which loop reads a file line by line safely?
warmup.a: `while IFS= read -r line; do ...; done < file`

warmup.q: How do you count ERROR lines in a log?
Which grep option hides lines that match?

problems.title: Errors with context: -n -A -B -C
problems.situation: The Spring Boot order service failed a payment. `grep ERROR` shows one line, but the real reason (the exception and the stack trace) is in the lines after it. The user also wants the line before each error.
task: Show ERROR lines with line numbers (`-n`).
Show each ERROR line plus the 3 lines after it (`-A 3`).
Show each ERROR line plus 1 line before it (`-B 1`).
Show 1 line before and after (`-C 1`) for `Timeout`, ignoring case.
hints: A = after, B = before, C = context (both sides).
grep prints `--` between groups that are not next to each other.
`grep -n -A 3 ERROR logs/orders.log`

explanation.meaning: Line numbers. Then the user can open the file at that line (`less +N file`).
Also print 3 lines After each match: the exception and the stack trace.
Also print 1 line Before each match: what happened just before.
Context: 1 line before and 1 after.
Separator between groups of lines that are far apart.

problems.expected_output:
4:2026-10-20 09:02:17 ERROR PaymentClient failed
9:2026-10-20 09:05:40 ERROR Database pool exhausted
=== -A 3 ===
2026-10-20 09:02:17 ERROR PaymentClient failed
java.net.SocketTimeoutException: Read timed out
    at PaymentClient.call(PaymentClient.java:42)
    at OrderService.pay(OrderService.java:88)
--
2026-10-20 09:05:40 ERROR Database pool exhausted
2026-10-20 09:05:41 INFO  pool size raised to 30
=== -B 1 ===
2026-10-20 09:02:16 WARN  retrying payment call
2026-10-20 09:02:17 ERROR PaymentClient failed
--
2026-10-20 09:03:00 INFO  GET /api/orders 200
2026-10-20 09:05:40 ERROR Database pool exhausted
=== -i -C 1 timeout ===
2026-10-20 09:02:17 ERROR PaymentClient failed
java.net.SocketTimeoutException: Read timed out
    at PaymentClient.call(PaymentClient.java:42)
mistakes: Writing `grep -A3B1`. Options with numbers must be separate: `grep -A 3 -B 1`.
Using `-c` together with `-A`: `-c` only counts and ignores the context.
problems.interview_say: When I search errors, I use `-A` and `-B` to see the stack trace and what happened before, and `-n` to know the line number.
problems.try_yourself: Run `grep -n -A 2 'Exception' logs/orders.log`. Then find which Java file and line number caused it.

problems.title: Search many files: -r -l -c -w
problems.situation: The old database server `db01` is being shut down. The user must find every config file that still uses it as `db_host`. Careful: `db011` is a different server, and a comment line only mentions `db01`.
task: Search all files in `configs/` for `db01` with `-r`. Look at the result.
Show only the file names with `-l`.
Use `-w` (whole word) for `db01`. `reports.conf` uses `db011`, but it is still listed. Why?
Count matches per file with `-c`.
Find only real settings: lines that start with `db_host=db01.`.
hints: `-r` = recursive (all files in all sub-folders).
`-w` matches only whole words: `db011` is not the word `db01`.
For the last step use an anchor and escape the dot: `grep -rl '^db_host=db01\.' configs`.

explanation.meaning: Search all files under a folder. Each line starts with `file:`.
Print only names of files that match (good for a to-do list).
Whole word only. `db011` no longer matches, but `reports.conf` stays in the list because its comment line has the whole word `db01`.
Count per file, also files with 0.
Line starts with `db_host=db01.`. `\.` is a real dot.
grep -r reads files in folder order, which can differ. `sort` makes the output stable.

problems.expected_output:
configs/orders.conf:db_host=db01.internal
configs/payments.conf:db_host=db01.internal
configs/reports.conf:db_host=db011.internal
configs/reports.conf:note: db01 is old
=== -l ===
configs/orders.conf
configs/payments.conf
configs/reports.conf
=== -w ===
configs/orders.conf
configs/payments.conf
configs/reports.conf
=== -c ===
configs/orders.conf:1
configs/payments.conf:1
configs/reports.conf:2
configs/sshd_config.copy:0
configs/web.conf:0
=== real settings ===
configs/orders.conf
configs/payments.conf
mistakes: Forgetting `-r` with a folder: `grep: configs: Is a directory`.
Searching `db01` without `-w` or anchors and changing `db011` by mistake in a bulk edit.
problems.interview_say: I use `grep -rl` to list the files that contain a string, `-w` to avoid partial matches, and anchors like `^` to match only real settings, not comments.
problems.try_yourself: Use `grep -rL db01 configs` (capital L). What does it list?

problems.title: Extract values with -o and -E
problems.situation: The API is slow. The user must pull out only the useful values from the access log: the IP addresses, the response times, and the slow requests over one second. `grep -o` prints only the matching part, not the whole line.
task: Print all IP addresses (only the IP) with `grep -oE`.
Count requests per IP (sorted).
Print only the `time=...ms` part of each line.
Show full lines where the time has 4 or more digits (1000 ms or more).
Count the 5xx status codes with a regex.
hints: IP pattern: `[0-9]{1,3}(\.[0-9]{1,3}){3}` (1-3 digits, then 3 times dot + 1-3 digits). Use it with `^` because the IP is at the start.
`{4,}` means 4 or more times: `time=[0-9]{4,}ms`.
Status codes are after the closing quote: `" 5[0-9]{2} `.

explanation.meaning: Print only the matching text, one match per line.
Extended regex: `+ ? {n,m} ( ) |` work without backslashes.
A digit, 1 to 3 times.
A group: a real dot and 1-3 digits, repeated 3 times.
One or more digits.
4 or more times, so 1000 and more.
Sort numbers, biggest first (Day 12).

mistakes: Without `-E`, `+` and `{3}` are normal characters in basic grep. `grep -o 'time=[0-9]+ms'` finds nothing.
Using `.` for a dot: `10.0.0.5` also matches `10a0b0c5`. Escape it: `10\.0\.0\.5`.
Forgetting the anchor: the IP pattern also finds numbers inside the date or URL in other logs.
problems.interview_say: I use `grep -oE` to extract only the values I need, like IPs or response times, then `sort | uniq -c` to count them. `-E` enables extended regex with `+`, `{n}` and groups.
problems.try_yourself: Extract only the numbers: `grep -oE 'time=[0-9]+' logs/access.log | grep -oE '[0-9]+'`. Then add them up in Day 11 with awk.

problems.title: Anchors and classes: only the real settings
problems.situation: A security audit asks: "Show the active SSH settings, without comments and empty lines." The file is a practice copy `configs/sshd_config.copy`. Comments can be indented. The user also checks for `PermitRootLogin`.
task: Print the file without empty lines (`^$`).
Print it without comment lines too. Use one `grep -Ev` with `^[[:space:]]*(#|$)`.
Print only lines that start with a capital letter (`^[A-Z]`).
Show the active `PermitRootLogin` line (not the commented one).
Find setting lines that end with a number (`[0-9]+$`).
hints: `^` = start of the line, `$` = end. `^$` = an empty line.
`[[:space:]]*` = zero or more spaces or tabs. It catches indented comments.
`grep '^PermitRootLogin'` does not match `#PermitRootLogin` because `#` is first.
solution: echo "=== no comments, no empty lines ==="
echo "=== lines starting with a capital ==="

explanation.meaning: An empty line: start and end with nothing between.
Line that is only spaces, or spaces then `#`. With `-v` these are removed.
One capital letter. `[[:upper:]]` is the same.
One or more digits at the end of the line.

problems.expected_output:
# Example SSH server config (practice copy)
Port 22
#PermitRootLogin yes
PermitRootLogin no
   # indented comment
PasswordAuthentication no
MaxAuthTries 3
=== no comments, no empty lines ===
Port 22
PermitRootLogin no
PasswordAuthentication no
MaxAuthTries 3
=== lines starting with a capital ===
Port 22
PermitRootLogin no
PasswordAuthentication no
MaxAuthTries 3
=== active PermitRootLogin ===
PermitRootLogin no
=== ends with a number ===
Port 22
MaxAuthTries 3
mistakes: Using `grep -v '#'`: it also removes setting lines that have a `#` later in the line.
Thinking `*` in regex means "any text" like in file globs. In regex, `.*` means any text.
problems.interview_say: To see active config lines I use `grep -Ev '^[[:space:]]*(#|$)' file`. It removes comments, indented comments and empty lines.
problems.try_yourself: On your real WSL, run the same command on `/etc/ssh/sshd_config` if it exists (read only, no sudo needed for most systems). Compare.

problems.title: Find the bug: the alert script
problems.situation: `alert.sh` feeds a Slack alert. It says `errors: 0` but there is an ERROR and a FATAL line. It shows requests from three "IPs" instead of one. And it counts only one timeout warning.
task: Run `bash alert.sh`. Compare with `cat logs/node.log`.
Find 3 bugs: the `|` in a basic regex, the dots in the IP, and the case of `timeout`.
Fix them. The expected result: errors 2, one line for 10.0.0.5, timeouts 2.
hints: In basic grep, `|` is a normal character. Use `-E`.
A `.` matches any character, and `10.0.0.5` is also inside `10.0.0.50`. Use `-F` (fixed text) and `-w` (whole word).
`Timeout` and `timeout`: add `-i`.
solution: # 1) count lines with ERROR or FATAL
# 2) show requests from the IP 10.0.0.5 only

explanation.meaning: Bug 1: basic grep looked for the text `ERROR|FATAL` literally, so the count was 0.
Bug 2: `-F` = fixed string (dots are dots), `-w` = whole word (not `10.0.0.50`).
Bug 3: count, ignore case: `Timeout` and `timeout`.

problems.expected_output:
errors: 0
2026-10-20 10:00:09 INFO request from 10.0.0.5
2026-10-20 10:00:10 INFO request from 10.0.0.50
2026-10-20 10:00:12 INFO request from 10a0b0c5
timeouts: 1
--- fixed ---
errors: 2
2026-10-20 10:00:09 INFO request from 10.0.0.5
timeouts: 2
mistakes: Escaping `\|` in basic grep works in GNU grep but not everywhere. `-E` is clearer and portable.
Only adding `-F` for the IP: `10.0.0.50` still matches. `-w` is needed too.
problems.interview_say: Three regex traps: `|` needs `-E`, a dot matches any character, and grep is case-sensitive. For IPs I use `grep -Fw`.
problems.try_yourself: Without `-F`, write a regex that matches only `10.0.0.5` as a whole word: `grep -E '\b10\.0\.0\.5\b'`.

problems.title: grep -F for text with special characters
problems.situation: A log uses `[ERROR]` in square brackets and shows prices with `$` and dots. In regex, `[ ]`, `$`, `.` and `*` have special meanings, so a normal grep finds the wrong lines. `-F` treats the pattern as plain text.
task: Run `grep '[ERROR]' special.txt`. Why does it also match the second line, which has no `[ERROR]`?
Run `grep -F '[ERROR]' special.txt`.
Find `$5.00` exactly with `-F`.
Find the text `a.b*c` exactly.
hints: `[ERROR]` in regex means "one of the letters E, R, O".
`-F` = fixed strings, no regex.
Use single quotes so bash does not touch `$5`.

explanation.meaning: A character class: any one of the letters E, R, O. The second line has `ERROR` without brackets, so it matches too.
Plain text search. Fast, and no character is special.
Single quotes: bash does not replace `$5` (the 5th argument).

problems.expected_output:
[ERROR] price is $5.00
ERROR price is 5x00
=== -F ===
[ERROR] price is $5.00
[ERROR] price is $5.00
path a.b*c found
mistakes: Double quotes: `grep -F "$5.00"` becomes `grep -F ".00"`, because `$5` is empty.
Escaping every character by hand: `\[ERROR\]` works, but `-F` is simpler and safer.

checks.run: set -- a b c d; grep -F "$5.00" special.txt

problems.interview_say: When I search for text with special characters like brackets, dots or dollars, I use `grep -F` with single quotes, so nothing is treated as regex.
problems.try_yourself: Put three IPs in a file `ips.txt`, one per line, and run `grep -Ff ips.txt logs/access.log`. `-f` reads many patterns from a file.

problems.title: Groups and alternation: (GET|POST) /api/(todos|users)
problems.situation: The team lead wants to know how many write requests (POST, PUT, DELETE) the to-do API had, and how many requests went to `/api/todos` with or without an id.
task: Count requests whose method is POST, PUT or DELETE with `grep -cE`.
Print only the method and path of every API request: `grep -oE '"(GET|POST|PUT|DELETE) /api/[^ ]*'`.
Match `/api/todos` and `/api/todos/7` with one pattern using `(/[0-9]+)?`.
hints: `(A|B|C)` = A or B or C (needs `-E`).
`[^ ]*` = any characters except a space.
`?` after a group = the group is optional.

explanation.meaning: Alternation inside a group: one of the three words.
Negated class: everything up to the next space (the path).
An optional group: `/7`, `/42` or nothing.
Delete the quote characters from the output (Day 12).

mistakes: Forgetting the space after the method in the pattern: `"(GET|POST)` also matches `"GETTER` in other logs.
Writing the group without `-E`: basic grep needs `\(` `\)` and `\|`.
problems.interview_say: With `grep -E` I use groups and `|` to match several words, and `?` to make a part optional, for example `/api/todos(/[0-9]+)?`.
problems.try_yourself: Count requests per method: `grep -oE '"[A-Z]+ ' logs/access.log | sort | uniq -c`.

interview.q: How do you show 5 lines after each error in a log?
interview.a: `grep -A 5 ERROR app.log`. `-B` shows lines before, `-C` lines on both sides.

interview.q: How do you list only the files that contain a word, in a whole folder?
interview.a: `grep -rl word folder/`. `-r` searches all files, `-l` prints only file names.
It prints only the matching part of each line, not the whole line. Good for extracting IPs or IDs.

interview.q: What is the difference between `grep`, `grep -E` and `grep -F`?
interview.a: `grep` uses basic regex. `-E` uses extended regex (`+`, `?`, `|`, `{n}`, groups). `-F` searches plain text, no regex at all.

interview.q: How do you remove comments and empty lines from a config file?

recap.meaning: Files that match / do not match
Start, end, any char, repeat, class, not-class
